input: A defect-reduction project that has recently been carried out on a packing line has delivered a meaningful improvement in the line's quality performance over the course of one quarter. The reject rate, which previously stood at 3.8%, has been brought down to 2.3%, corresponding to a reduction of 1.5 percentage points. When this improvement is set against the line's output of 304k units per year, it can be seen that the change avoids approximately 4560 rejected units each year, which represents a considerable saving in wasted product and in rework. It is worth noting, in the interests of balance, that the quarter in question did include a planned shutdown of the line, and that the rates reported here have not been adjusted in order to take that shutdown into account. This caveat does not detract from the progress that has been achieved; it does, however, mean that the full picture will only become clear once a further quarter of operation, unaffected by any shutdown, has been completed, at which point the figures can be compared on a truly like-for-like basis and the improvement confirmed as a lasting one. The project team is to be commended for the progress that has been recorded here, and the position will be reviewed once again when the figures for the further quarter are available for consideration.
target: The packing line cut its reject rate from 3.8% to 2.3% over one quarter, a reduction of 1.5 percentage points. At 304k units per year, the change avoids about 4560 rejected units per year. The figures are the project's own comparison: the rate recorded before the project and the rate recorded after it, on the same line, with the avoided units computed at the current annual volume. The avoided units follow from the rate difference at that volume, and they are the whole of the benefit the project is credited with; effects on cost, on rework labour and on output are outside this comparison and are not claimed here. One qualification stands on the rates themselves. The quarter in which the new rate was recorded included a planned shutdown, and the rates are not adjusted for it. A shutdown quarter is not a typical quarter: the line stops and restarts, and the running periods either side of the stop carry a different mix of work from a full quarter's running. The recorded reduction is therefore the reduction of that quarter, and a further quarter without a shutdown is the evidence that would show whether the new rate holds in ordinary operation. Until that evidence exists, the avoided-units figure carries the same qualification as the rate difference it is computed from. The project is therefore credited with a real but provisionally evidenced improvement, and the credit stands to be confirmed or revised by the rates of the quarter that follows.
